chief_complaint: exertional syncope, severe shortness of breath when climbing stairs, and angina in elderly man with loud systolic murmur
hpi_details: 75M presents with 6-month history of worsening dyspnea on exertion and chest tightness when walking up inclines. Yesterday experienced sudden loss of consciousness (syncope) while carrying groceries up steps, recovering fully within 2 minutes without neuro deficits. Reports sleeping on 3 pillows due to orthopnea.
ideas: thinks he is getting old and out of shape or having minor dizzy spells
concerns: worried because he fainted on the stairs and could have broken his neck
expectations: wants his heart valves checked and fixed so he can walk without blacking out

clinical_knowledge.topic: Severe Symptomatic Calcific Aortic Stenosis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Severe Symptomatic Calcific Aortic Stenosis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Admit for urgent heart team multidisciplinary evaluation (Cardiothoracic Surgery and Interventional Cardiology), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: exertional syncope, severe shortness of breath when climbing stairs, and angina in elderly man with loud systolic murmur

Key HPI features: 75M presents with 6-month history of worsening dyspnea on exertion and chest tightness when walking up inclines. Yesterday experienced sudden loss of consciousness (syncope) while carrying groceries up steps, recovering fully within 2 minutes without neuro deficits. Reports sleeping on 3 pillows due to orthopnea.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 68, BP 112/82 (narrow pulse pressure). Carotid upstrokes delayed and diminished in amplitude (pulsus parvus et tardus). Auscultation reveals a harsh, Grade 4/6 late-peaking crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur loudest at right second intercostal space radiating to bilateral carotid arteries, with diminished/absent A2 heart sound. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirms Severe Calcific Aortic Stenosis: peak aortic jet velocity 4.6 m/s, mean transvalvular gradient 52 mmHg, and aortic valve area (AVA) 0.65 cm2 (normal > 2.0 cm2). Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) 48%.
Relevant background/PMH: Hypertension, Chronic Kidney Disease Stage 3a
Current medications: Lisinopril 20mg daily, Furosemide 20mg daily
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Severe Symptomatic Calcific Aortic Stenosis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Coronary artery disease alone without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Exertional syncope — one of the three classic symptoms and a marker of high mortality risk if untreated.
management_principles: Admit for urgent heart team multidisciplinary evaluation (Cardiothoracic Surgery and Interventional Cardiology)
Perform pre-operative coronary angiography and CT TAVR protocol
Given age 75, CKD, and anatomy, evaluate suitability for Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement (TAVR) vs Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement (SAVR)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease

reference_soap.subjective: 75M presenting with classic symptomatic triad of severe aortic stenosis: angina, syncope, and heart failure (dyspnea/orthopnea).
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 68, BP 112/82 (narrow pulse pressure). Carotid upstrokes delayed and diminished in amplitude (pulsus parvus et tardus). Auscultation reveals a harsh, Grade 4/6 late-peaking crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur loudest at right second intercostal space radiating to bilateral carotid arteries, with diminished/absent A2 heart sound. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirms Severe Calcific Aortic Stenosis: peak aortic jet velocity 4.6 m/s, mean transvalvular gradient 52 mmHg, and aortic valve area (AVA) 0.65 cm2 (normal > 2.0 cm2). Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) 48%.
reference_soap.assessment: Severe Symptomatic Calcific Aortic Valve Stenosis with poor prognosis without mechanical intervention.
reference_soap.plan: Admit for urgent heart team multidisciplinary evaluation (Cardiothoracic Surgery and Interventional Cardiology). Perform pre-operative coronary angiography and CT TAVR protocol. Given age 75, CKD, and anatomy, evaluate suitability for Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement (TAVR) vs Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement (SAVR). Avoid hypotension and use diuretics or vasodilators cautiously with monitoring when clinically necessary.

learning_objectives: Recognize the classic prognostic triad of severe aortic stenosis (angina = 5 yr survival, syncope = 3 yr survival, heart failure = 2 yr survival without replacement)
Correlate physical exam findings (pulsus parvus et tardus, late-peaking systolic murmur radiating to carotids, absent A2) with hemodynamic severity of AS
Interpret echocardiographic thresholds for severe aortic stenosis (jet velocity > 4.0 m/s, mean gradient > 40 mmHg, AVA < 1.0 cm2)
Compare Heart Team selection criteria between TAVR and SAVR based on surgical risk and anatomical factors

teaching.one_liner: Progressive calcification narrows the aortic valve, and once symptoms appear — exertional breathlessness, angina, or syncope — prognosis is poor without valve replacement (surgical or transcatheter).
red_flags: Exertional syncope — one of the three classic symptoms and a marker of high mortality risk if untreated

must_ask.say: Do you get chest tightness, breathlessness, or dizziness when you exert yourself?
Tell me exactly what happened when you fainted on the stairs.
How many pillows do you need to sleep comfortably?
How has your breathlessness changed over the past six months?
What worries you most about the fainting episode?

history.answer: I passed out on my front steps yesterday while carrying groceries, and I have been getting terribly short of breath whenever I walk.
Yesterday afternoon, I was carrying a heavy grocery bag up the steps to my house when everything went dark all of a sudden.
Yes, it happened right in the middle of hauling groceries up the stairs, not while I was sitting or resting.
I did not have any cold sweats, nausea, or ringing in my ears beforehand; I just felt lightheaded for a split second and collapsed.
My chest was feeling tight and squeezed as I climbed the steps right before I blacked out.
I was panting heavily and completely out of breath from walking up the incline before I collapsed.
No, my heart was not racing, skipping beats, or pounding in my chest before it happened.
No, I was not standing in the heat, straining to use the bathroom, coughing hard, or getting up quickly from bed.
My neighbor was nearby and saw me drop; he said I was completely unconscious for about one to two minutes.
He told me my body did not shake or stiffen up, and I did not bite my tongue or lose control of my bladder.
I came around quickly and knew who and where I was right away, without feeling foggy or drowsy.
I scraped my left elbow on the railing on the way down, but fortunately I did not hit my head or break anything.
No, I did not have any weakness in my arms or legs, numbness, slurred speech, or blurred vision.
I have had a couple of lightheaded spells over the past few months when walking uphill, but yesterday was the very first time I completely blacked out.
For about six months now, walking up inclines and stairs has been getting harder and harder because of chest tightness and breathlessness.
I have had to sleep propped up on three pillows recently because I feel smothered if I try to lie flat on my back.
No, I have not had any nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or dark black bowel movements.
I do not have diabetes and do not take insulin, and I had eaten a hearty lunch about an hour before this happened.
I have been taking the exact same prescriptions for years, and my doctor has not added or changed anything recently.
I have never had a heart attack, but my doctor mentioned a few years ago that he heard a heart murmur.
I am terrified because I collapsed right on the concrete steps, and if I had fallen backward, I could have broken my neck or died.
I keep telling myself I might just be getting old and out of shape, but I want my heart valves checked and fixed so I can walk safely.
I have had high blood pressure for about fifteen years and stage three chronic kidney disease that my doctor keeps an eye on.
I had an appendectomy when I was in my twenties, but I have never had any heart surgery or hospital stays for chest pain.
I take lisinopril twenty milligrams once a day and furosemide twenty milligrams once a day in the morning.
I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I smoked about a pack a day for twenty-five years, but I quit completely twenty years ago and haven't touched a cigarette since.
I might have a single beer on the weekend once or twice a month, but I do not drink heavily.
I am a retired auto mechanic, and I live at home with my wife in a two-story house.
My father died of a stroke at age eighty-two and my mother had osteoarthritis, but nobody in my family had sudden unexplained deaths or young heart attacks.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 112/82 mmHg, heart rate is 68 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, body temperature is 36.7 degrees Celsius, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air.
Supine blood pressure is 112/82 mmHg with a heart rate of 68 beats per minute; standing blood pressure is 110/80 mmHg with a heart rate of 72 beats per minute, showing no orthostatic drop.
Alert, well-appearing elderly male in no acute distress, with no scalp lacerations, contusions, or external signs of head trauma.
Radial pulses are regular and equal bilaterally, while carotid upstrokes are noticeably delayed and diminished in volume bilaterally.
A harsh, grade 4/6 late-peaking crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur is loudest at the right second intercostal space radiating to both carotids, with a diminished A2 heart sound.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with normal vesicular breath sounds and no wheezes or crackles.
Jugular venous pulsations are visible approximately 2 cm above the sternal angle at 45 degrees, without pathological distention.
Oral mucosa is moist and pink without lateral tongue lacerations, abrasions, or bite marks.
Cranial nerves two through twelve are grossly intact with symmetric facial movements and clear, articulate speech.
Motor strength is 5/5 in all four extremities with normal muscle bulk and tone.
There is trace bilateral pretibial pitting edema with no calf tenderness or asymmetry.
